origins.name: Abdellah Zakibrug
origins.en: Abdellah Zaki (ntb 1936 – Lelystad, 2017) was a Dutch-Moroccan artist with a love of history and culture. His work focused mostly on flowers and Amsterdam cityscapes. The naming also symbolises labour migration and the connection between two cultures.

origins.name: Ad Grimmonbrug
origins.en: Ad (Adriaan Alphonsus Maria) Grimmon (1883-1953). As a furniture maker, (interior) architect and colour specialist, he moved from the craft tradition of the Amsterdamse School towards industrial modernism. His career spanned the first half of the 20th century.

origins.name: Albert Helmanbrug
origins.en: Albert Helman is the pseudonym of Lodewijk Alphonsus Maria Lichtveld (1903-1996). He was a Dutch-Surinamese writer, politician and resistance fighter. His best-known novels are Zuid-Zuidwest (South-Southwest) from 1926 and De stille Plantage (The Silent Plantation) from 1931. He received an honorary doctorate from the Universiteit van Amsterdam and died in Buitenveldert.

origins.name: Aldo van Eyckbrug
origins.en: Aldo van Eyck (1918-1999) is best known as the architect of the Burgerweeshuis on the nearby IJsbaanpad. His colleagues named him 'Dutch architect of the century'.

origins.name: Aluminiumbrug
origins.en: This drawbridge is called Aluminiumbrug because in 1956 its leaf (the bridge deck) was made of aluminium, the first in the Netherlands. Another name for it was Dwingerbrug, after the neighbouring bastion 'Swijght Utrecht'.

origins.name: Amstelstroombrug
origins.en: The bridge is named after the avenue. The Amstelstroomlaan is named after a former country house (estate) on the Amsteldijk, demolished in 1916. A house already stood here in 1583, and it was known by the name Amstelstroom.

origins.name: Angenietje Swarthofbrug
origins.en: Around 1800, Amsterdam had thousands of foundlings. They were placed in the care of the Aalmoezeniersweeshuis on the Prinsengracht (near the bridge), which boarded them out with wet nurses in the city. These were women who wanted to add a wet nurse's wage to their household income. Angenietje Swart was one of them. In all, she cared for 126 children.

origins.name: Anna Paulownabrug
origins.en: Anna Paulowna (1795-1865) married the Hereditary Prince of Orange, later King William II, on 21 February 1816. Through this marriage she received the title of Hereditary Princess. After William I abdicated on 7 October 1840, William II was inaugurated on 28 November in the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam. Under Anna's influence, court life took on a more royal grandeur. Although her upbringing gave her a distant and sometimes haughty manner as queen, she was deeply involved in Dutch society. She had learned Dutch from the court teacher Arie van der Spuij and spoke it better than her husband, with whom she usually spoke French. Even as Hereditary Princess she worked with conviction for 'the people'.

origins.name: Anna van Saksenbrug
origins.en: Named after Anna van Saksen (1544-1577), the second wife of Willem van Oranje and mother of Prince Maurits and Princess Anna.

origins.name: Annemie Wolffbrug
origins.en: The photographer Anna Maria Koller was known as Annemie Wolff and also used the pseudonym Marianne (Germany, 27 December 1906 - Amsterdam, 2 February 1994). In Munich she married the architect and photographer Helmuth Egon Wilhelm Wolff (1895-1940). In May 1933 they fled to Amsterdam, because as a Jew Helmuth could no longer work in Germany and a warrant had been issued for his arrest on false grounds. On the night of 14 to 15 May 1940, Annemie and Helmuth tried to take their own lives. They were found and taken to the Nederlands Israëlitisch Ziekenhuis, where Helmuth died. As a young widow of 35, Annemie had to get her life back on track.

origins.name: Anton Jolingbrug
origins.en: Antonius Jacobus Joling (1857-1934), architect. He learned his trade under Pierre Cuypers (1827-1921) and set up on his own around 1887. He mainly designed public buildings such as offices, hospitals and schools. The Peek & Cloppenburg building on the Dam is by Joling.

origins.name: Arlandabrug
origins.en: Name of Stockholm's airport.

origins.name: Armand Sunierbrug
origins.en: Armand Louis Jean Sunier (Rotterdam, 17 December 1886 – Baarn, 13 May 1974) was a Dutch biologist and the third director of the Natura Artis Magistra zoo. Sunier prevented the deportation of staff and animals to Germany and turned a blind eye to people hiding in the zoo. He was also one of the key figures in the breeding programme set up to save the wisent (European bison) from extinction. In addition, he was a member of the International Union of Directors of Zoological Gardens for many years and briefly served as its president.

origins.name: Armbrug
origins.en: The seventh bridge over the Oudezijls Voorburgwal. The middle section of this wooden bridge at the O.Z. Armsteeg could be raised. It was rebuilt in 1882 and renewed in 1906.

origins.name: Aron Wolff Berlijnbrug
origins.en: Composer and conductor (1817-1870). He wrote more than two hundred works, including at least twenty large romantic ballets for the Stadschouwburg, where he was orchestra master from 1846.

origins.name: Baanbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Lijnbaansgracht, which used to be called the Baangracht.

origins.name: Bantammerbrug
origins.en: The name of this fixed bridge recalls the sixteenth century, when the Dutch brought goods from Bantam (Dutch East Indies) to Amsterdam.

origins.name: Batavus Droogstoppelbrug
origins.en: Batavus Droogstoppel is a fictional character in Multatuli's Max Havelaar. He is a coffee broker at Lauriergracht 37. Multatuli portrays him as a 'wretched product of filthy greed and blasphemous sanctimony'.

origins.name: Beemsterstraatbrug
origins.en: Named after the street beneath it.

origins.name: Beltbrug
origins.en: Recalls the municipal rubbish dump (vuilnisbelt) that was in use there until 1888.

origins.name: Berensluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Berenstraat, on which it lies. In the seventeenth century, the tanneries and the hide trade were located in the adjacent part of what is now the Jordaan.

origins.name: Berlagebrug
origins.en: Hendrik Petrus Berlage (1856-1934), architect. His buildings include the Koopmansbeurs on the Damrak. He designed the southern expansion plan (uitbreidingsplan-Zuid) and the Mercatorplein and its surroundings. His last creation was the Berlagebrug (1932). In 1966 Hildo Krop made a statue of him, which was placed on the Victorieplein.

origins.name: Berta de Vriesbrug
origins.en: Luberta de Hondt de Vries, known as Berta de Vries (Amsterdam, 23 January 1885 – Amsterdam, 19 April 1959), was active in the revolutionary socialist women's movement, the Communistische Partij in Nederland and the Amsterdams Speeltuinverbond.

origins.name: Beudekerbrug
origins.en: Frans Beudeker (1815-1897) was director of the Stads-bestedelingenhuis, a municipal home for people who could not look after themselves. In the nineteenth century, 'Hij gaat naar Beudeker' (he's going to Beudeker) was an expression for someone who had become dependent on care. The Stads-bestedelingenhuis was later converted into the Paleis van Justitie, which stands right next to this bridge.

origins.name: Blauwbrug
origins.en: The name of this fixed bridge recalls an earlier version of it, which after the Alteration of Amsterdam in 1578 was painted in the blue of Nassau. The present bridge dates from 1884. Its architects, B. de Greef and W. Springer, took their inspiration from a bridge over the Seine. Another name for this bridge was Sophiabrug, but through all the changes the name Blauwbrug was kept. That other name for the Blauwbrug never caught on, just as Sophiaplein never did for the Muntplein. Sophia of Württemberg (1817-1877) was the first wife of King Willem III, who opened this renewed bridge in 1839.

origins.name: Boerenweteringbrug
origins.en: The name of the watercourse that originally ran from the Kalfjeslaan to what is now the Koningsplein. It was formerly also called the Oude Wetering, as opposed to the Nieuwe Wetering (Kostverlorenvaart). The Weteringbuurt and the Weteringschans take their names from this wetering (drainage canal).

origins.name: Boy Edgarbrug
origins.en: George Willem Fred (Boy) Edgar (1915-1980), composer and arranger of light entertainment music, and a doctor by training. His compositions added a great deal to the repertoire of light music.

origins.name: Buiksloterdraaibrug
origins.en: The Buikslotermeerpolder, a lake drained in 1628.

origins.name: Bullebak
origins.en: The bullebak was a mythical water bogeyman that haunted not only the old little lock near the Haarlemmerplein but also the stone vault that joined the Bloemgracht to the Buitensingel (bridge 160). According to legend, the monster lay in wait there to drag into the water any passer-by who ventured too close to the edge.

origins.name: Camera Obscurabrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the book Camera Obscura, published in 1839 by Hildebrand, the pseudonym of Nicolaas Beets (1814-1903).

origins.name: Caroline Herschelbrug
origins.en: Caroline Herschel (Hanover, 1750 - Hanover, 1848) was involved in building and grinding the lenses of the very largest telescopes of the eighteenth century, and she discovered and described nebulae not observed before. Caroline Herschel also made many observations of her own. She was the first woman with a paid scientific post.

origins.name: Cecilia van Alphen-Jagtmanbrug
origins.en: Cecilia Maria Cornelia Jagtman (1910-1972) and her husband Pieter van Alphen (1909-1953) were active members of the CPN (Communist Party). During the Second World War, at the risk of their lives, they produced and distributed the clandestine newspaper De Waarheid, among others. He was arrested by the Nazis in April 1941. She carried on the work, and also hid people in her house at Fresiastraat 12 in Amsterdam-Noord.

origins.name: Ceintuurbrug
origins.en: At the end of the nineteenth century a ring road (ceintuurweg, or belt) was laid around a large part of the city. The stretch between the Boerenwetering and the Amstel was later named Ceintuurbaan. The other stretches later got other names, because a section in between was not yet part of Amsterdam at the time.

origins.name: Charley Tooropbrug
origins.en: Charley Toorop (1891-1955) developed her own style, Expressive Objective Realism (Expressief Zakelijk Realisme). She is widely regarded as the most powerful woman in twentieth-century Dutch painting.

origins.name: Corry Tendeloobrug
origins.en: Nancy Sophie Cornélie Tendeloo (1897-1956), politician, feminist and lawyer. City councillor for the Vrijzinnig Democratische Bond (VDB) from 1938 to 1941, and from 1945 to 1956 a member of the House of Representatives for the VDB and then the PvdA. Among other things, in 1955 she moved to end the dismissal of married women from government service, which happened a year later.

origins.name: Dageraadsbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the former shipyard 'De Dageraad' (the dawn) nearby.

origins.name: De Duifbrug
origins.en: Named after the church De Duif (the dove) at Prinsengracht 754, officially called the Sint Willibrordus binnen de Veste.

origins.name: Dick Schmüllbrug
origins.en: Diederich Herman 'Dick' Schmüll (Sumatra, 1908 - Amsterdam, 1990) founded the Dutch Basketball Federation and the Dutch Volleyball Federation.

origins.name: Dirk de Waterduikerbrug
origins.en: Dirk Rietveldt (1858-1940) rescued many people (perhaps as many as 74), dogs and cats from the water of Amsterdam's canals. That made him a highly respected figure in the Jordaan, and he received several medals from the city of Amsterdam for humanity. In the immediate surroundings of this bridge, three courtyards are named after men who also rescued many from drowning: Doris Rijkers, Jan Cupido and Frans Naerebout.

origins.name: Doelensluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge takes its name from the Kloveniersdoelen. The doelen were the places where the civic militia guilds met and practised shooting at a target (doel). These doelen had their seat by the tower Swych Utrecht (where the Doelen Hotel is now). They practised on the grounds of the Old Convent of the Nuns (the Binnengasthuis site).

origins.name: Dr. Samuel de Ranitzbrug
origins.en: Doctor (1834-1913), in practice in Amsterdam from 1861. Moved by the wretched conditions of many sick Amsterdam children, in 1865 he decided to found what later became the Emma Children's Hospital. In 1873 the institution moved to the Sarphatistraat, not far from this bridge, where it stayed for 117 years.

origins.name: Drieharingenbrug
origins.en: This drawbridge takes its name from the three herrings above the door of the house 'De Drie Haringen' (the three herrings) at Vierwindendwarsstraat no. 1.

origins.name: Drs. P-brug
origins.en: Drs. P (Thun, 24 August 1919 - Amsterdam, 13 June 2015), pseudonym of Heinz Hermann Polzer, was a Dutch-language lyricist of Swiss nationality. His stage name, thought up by Willem Duys, refers to the academic degree of doctorandus (abbreviated drs.) in economics that Polzer took at the Nederlandsche Economische Hoogeschool (now Erasmus University). He was also a poet, writer, cabaret artist, man of letters, composer, pianist and singer of his own songs.

origins.name: Duizendste Brug
origins.en: On 2 April 1974 this bridge was opened as Amsterdam's thousandth bridge by alderman Han Lammers.

origins.name: Elsje Christiaensbrug
origins.en: Elsje Christiaens was an 18-year-old Danish girl who was strangled on the Dam in 1664 because she had killed her landlady with an axe. She was hanged on the gallows field.

origins.name: Enneüs Heermabrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after Enneüs Heerma (1944-1999). He was an alderman of Amsterdam for the CDA from 1978 to 1986. He then became state secretary, first for Foreign Trade and later for Housing. From 1994 to 1997 he led the CDA group in the House of Representatives.

origins.name: Etty Hillesumbrug
origins.en: Etty Hillesum (Middelburg, 15 January 1914 - Auschwitz, c. 30 November 1943) was a Jewish writer who wrote her diaries in the first years of the Second World War.

origins.name: Eva Schalkbrug
origins.en: Eva Schalk (1890-1978) was the first woman on a water board. She was for 27 years a hoofdingeland (board member) of the Buikslotermeer polder and for 21 years a hoofdingeland of the Hoogheemraadschap (regional water board).

origins.name: Ezelsbrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge (donkey bridge) recalls the hard struggle the residents had to wage against the car lobby, which would rather have seen bridges for ordinary traffic here. They often felt like donkeys that kept stumbling over the same stone. The name also refers to the memory aid called an ezelsbruggetje (a mnemonic). The bridge was officially opened on 14 March 1987 by having a donkey walk across it.

origins.name: Fré Cohenbrug
origins.en: Frederika Sophia Cohen (1903-1943), graphic artist, whose brochures, covers, bindings and other work gave 1930s design its face. She worked for the Amsterdam city printing office from 1929 to 1941, giving her own twist to influences from Jugendstil, the Amsterdam School and De Stijl. She went on working while in hiding until she was betrayed.

origins.name: Galgenbrug
origins.en: The name (gallows bridge) refers to the view from this bridge of the gallows of the Volewijk, which stood there until 1795.

origins.name: Geert Geertsenbrug
origins.en: Geert Geertsen was the birth name of Desiderius Erasmus (1467-1536). Because his Dutch name is linked to the word begeerte (desire), he took the Latin word for desire as his first name and the Greek word as his surname.

origins.name: George Madurobrug
origins.en: George John Lionel Maduro (1916-1945) was a resistance man of Antillean descent who died in the Dachau concentration camp. The miniature city of Madurodam in The Hague is named after him.

origins.name: Ger van Zanenbrug
origins.en: Ger van Zanen (1929-2015) was a passionate nature lover and from 1960 until his death a member of the Royal Dutch Natural History Society, Amsterdam (KNNV). Under his leadership a great deal of field-biology research and surveying was done in Amsterdam. Ger van Zanen was always ready to show anyone interested the way in nature. The bridge leads from the housing area to the Ruige Riet, a valuable, still untouched nature area that is part of the Sloterpark. The area is rich in mushrooms, among other things, and people on mushroom walks mostly cross the bridge and will all remember Ger van Zanen.

origins.name: Gerda Tarobrug
origins.en: Gerda Taro (1910-1937) was the first woman photographer at the front. She fought against Nazism, and her passion has made her a symbol of anti-fascism.

origins.name: Gerrie Mührenbrug
origins.en: Gerrie Mühren (Volendam, 2 February 1946 - Volendam, 19 September 2013), footballer. In a 22-year career he played for Volendam, Ajax, Real Betis, MVV, Seiko SA and DS '79. With Ajax he won the European Cup three times and the Dutch league three times. He played ten times for the Netherlands.

origins.name: Gierzwaluwbrug
origins.en: The common swift (Apus apus) is a very special bird. Swifts spend almost their whole lives in the air: they eat, drink, mate and even sleep on the wing! They land only in spring at a fixed nest site, usually under roof tiles. They breed in almost every city in Europe, including the centre of Amsterdam, and catch mainly midges in flight. They are enormously fast and agile in the air, but once landed on the nest they can only shuffle on their short legs. In the Bijlmerweide by the G-buurt, seven bridges have been given bird names beginning with G. City ecologists gave a workshop about birds to children from the local Kidsclub, who then chose their favourite species.

origins.name: Goudvinkbrug
origins.en: The bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is perhaps the most beautiful bird in the country. Males and females both have a black head. The male can be recognised by his bright rose-red belly and cheeks. Bullfinches are in this park all year round, but despite their bright colours they are hard to see. Many inconspicuous little brown birds sing beautifully, but this handsome bird can only make squeaking sounds. You can't have everything. In the Bijlmerweide by the G-buurt, seven bridges have been given bird names beginning with G. City ecologists gave a workshop about birds to children from the local Kidsclub, who then chose their favourite species.

origins.name: Grimnessesluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the water called the Grim (muddy ditch), which formed the city's southern boundary from 1342 to about 1400.

origins.name: Groene spechtbrug
origins.en: The green woodpecker (Picus viridis) hacks a hole in a tree to make its nest. Hacking it out takes more than two weeks, so they often use an existing hole. Green woodpeckers have a very long, sticky tongue with which they can lick insects out from behind the bark. But they mainly eat ants, on the ground. You can recognise them easily by their moss-green back and the red cap on their head. A funny fact: they can also laugh very loudly! In the Bijlmerweide by the G-buurt, seven bridges have been given bird names beginning with G. City ecologists gave a workshop about birds to children from the local Kidsclub, who then chose their favourite species.

origins.name: Groentemarktbrug
origins.en: Named after the vegetable market held near here until 1934. In that year the trade moved to the Centrale Markthallen.

origins.name: Groentepraambrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge recalls the time when many vegetable barges sailed from the west via the Admiralengrachten and the Kostverlorenkade to the Marnixstraat, where the vegetables were traded. Pramen are low little boats that can easily pass through polder ditches and under footbridges.

origins.name: Gwijde van Henegouwenbrug
origins.en: Also Guy of Avesnes, or Gui d'Avesnes (1253-1317), Bishop of Utrecht. He personally administered the possessions of the Lords of Amstel. Just before his consecration in Utrecht, in 1300 or 1301, he granted Amsterdam its town rights.

origins.name: Haardsteebrug
origins.en: The name of a farm near Steenderen (Gelderland).

origins.name: Haarlemmersluis
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Haarlemmerstraat, the road out of Amsterdam to Haarlem.

origins.name: Halvemaansbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge takes its name from the Halvemaansteeg. The origin of that name may lie in the façade of Halvemaansteeg no. 18, marked 'Van Ouds de Halve Maan' (of old the Half Moon).

origins.name: Han Lammersbrug
origins.en: Han Lammers (1931-2000) worked as a journalist for the ANP, the Algemeen Dagblad and De Groene Amsterdammer before becoming a city councillor and alderman in Amsterdam for the PvdA in 1970. In 1965, with Jan Nagel among others, he was involved in founding the renewal movement Nieuw Links (New Left). As alderman for urban development, Lammers set urban renewal in motion. He had plans drawn up to demolish whole neighbourhoods: from the Jordaan to the Dapperbuurt, completely new districts were to be built from scratch, with a quite different street plan. Residents formed action groups, which in the end successfully fought this model of urban renewal.

origins.name: Han van Zomerenbrug
origins.en: Han van Zomeren (1920-1941) was a graphic artist active in the resistance during the German occupation. He printed pamphlets calling for resistance. He was executed by firing squad on the Laren heath in 1941 and reburied in the Field of Honour in Overveen in 1952.

origins.name: Hannie Schaftbrug
origins.en: Hannie Schaft (1920-1945) was a Haarlem communist and resistance fighter, known as the Girl with the Red Hair. She carried out several attacks on Germans and collaborators, and for that she was shot dead by the Germans in the dunes near Bloemendaal on 17 April 1945. On 27 November 1945 her body was reburied in the Field of Honour at Bloemendaal in Overveen.

origins.name: Hanny Michaelisbrug
origins.en: Hanny Michaelis (Amsterdam, 19 December 1922 - Amsterdam, 11 June 2007) was a poet, writer and translator. She made her debut in 1949 with Klein voorspel (little prelude). Up to 1971 five more collections of new poems appeared. She also wrote (autobiographical) prose and made a number of translations.

origins.name: Hans Kressebrug
origins.en: Hans Kresse was an important comic artist and a born Amsterdammer, who became known for his comic strips of Eric de Noorman (Eric the Norseman). Kresse made many comics and stories based on history that became world-famous.

origins.name: Haringpakkersbrug
origins.en: While in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the herring sellers mostly lived on the Nieuwendijk, this and other alleys along that dike were home to the herring packers. Until 1913 the alley was called Kapelsteeg, but it was then renamed Haringpakkerssteeg because of confusion with the other Kapelstegen.

origins.name: Hartmanbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the tobacconist André Hartman, who was killed in a robbery at his shop on 6 November 1993. The bridge is also a tribute to his wife An Hartman and to all shopkeepers who do their work in dangerous circumstances.

origins.name: Heibrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Heisteeg, on which it lies. The Heisteeg takes its name from a corner house called 't Hayblok, already mentioned at the beginning of the sixteenth century. Until 1606 an unofficial name for this bridge was Strontenburgerbrug (roughly, dung-town bridge), because of the nuisance caused by two nearby shipyards.

origins.name: Hein Donnerbrug
origins.en: Jan Hein Donner (1927-1988) was a chess grandmaster who was Dutch champion several times. He was also a polemicist and a columnist for NRC Handelsblad.

origins.name: Hennetjesbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge was probably once a narrow wooden chicken bridge (hennetje: little hen).

origins.name: Henrietta Leavittbrug
origins.en: Henrietta Swan Leavitt (1868-1921), American astronomer. She discovered a relationship between the brightness and the period of pulsation of certain stars. Her discovery let astronomers calculate for the first time the distance between distant galaxies and the earth. Her work also formed the basis for calculating the expanding universe.

origins.name: Henriëtte van Heukelom-van den Brandelerbrug
origins.en: Hendrika Jacoba van den Brandeler-Heukelom (1884-1985), composer and pianist, a pupil of Dirk Schäfer (1873-1931) among others. Her works include songs, a requiem for her father, and a Stabat Mater performed by the Concertgebouw Orchestra in 1913.

origins.name: Horst Blankenburgbrug
origins.en: Horst Blankenburg, born 10 July 1947 in Heidenheim an der Brenz (Germany). Twice Dutch champion, twice KNVB Cup winner, three times winner of the European Cup, twice winner of the European Super Cup and once winner of the Intercontinental Cup, he played 188 league matches for Ajax. In 1969 Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final of the prestigious European Cup, today's Champions League. Ajax lost that final, but two years later, in 1971, won the most important prize in football after all. In the two following years Ajax retained the title, confirming itself as the standard-bearer of Dutch football.

origins.name: Hortusbrug
origins.en: After the Hortus Botanicus opposite.

origins.name: Hugo de Vriesbrug
origins.en: Botanist (1848-1935), professor at the University of Amsterdam from 1880 to 1918. He developed mutation theory, which holds that characteristics change in jumps. The theory applies to all living organisms, not only plants.

origins.name: Huntumbrug
origins.en: A patrician house on the Vecht, south of Vreeland.

origins.name: Ina Boekbinderbrug
origins.en: Ina Boekbinder (Assen, 1915 - Hilversum, 1987) was a Jewish resistance fighter in the Second World War. She helped Jewish children go into hiding and delivered ration coupons to people in hiding. She also carried Sten guns in her bicycle bags and raided a bandage depot.

origins.name: Isa van Eeghenbrug
origins.en: Isabelle Henriette van Eeghen (1913-1996), archivist and historian. Between 1944 and 1978, at the City Archives near this bridge, she produced many works, among them a substantial study of Amsterdam's booksellers. She arranged the purchase of Jacob Olie's (1834-1905) photograph collection. A board member of the Genootschap Amstelodamum, she received the Silver Medal (Zilveren Penning) in 1971.

origins.name: Isaac Israëlsbrug
origins.en: Isaac Israëls (1865-1934) was the son of Jozef Israëls (1824-1911) and also a painter. With George Breitner, Willem Witsen, Jac. van Looy and Jan Eduard Karsen he was a representative of the Amsterdam school of painting. He painted factory girls and impressions of the city, among other things. At the 1928 Olympic Games in Amsterdam he won a gold Olympic art medal in painting for his picture 'De Rode Ruiter' (the red rider). This bridge connects to the Breitnerstraat and lies near the Willem Witsenstraat.

origins.name: Jacoba van Tongerenbrug
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1903-1967). As a social worker she took part in clandestine activities such as courier work, and then founded Groep 2000, an organisation of 140 people that helped up to 4500 people in hiding. She was nicknamed 'De bonnenkoningin' (the coupon queen) for smuggling ration coupons in a special waistcoat. She received the Yad Vashem distinction in 1990.

origins.name: Jan Evertsenbrug
origins.en: Johan Evertsen (1600-1666), of a Zeeland family of naval heroes. As admiral he took part in several naval battles, including the Battle of the Downs (1639). He was killed in the Second Anglo-Dutch War.

origins.name: Jan Schaeferbrug
origins.en: Johannes Lodewijk Nicolaas Schaefer (1940-1994), politician for the Labour Party (PvdA). He sat in the House of Representatives from 1971, was state secretary for urban renewal at the Ministry of Housing and Spatial Planning in the Den Uyl cabinet from 1973 to 1977, and alderman in Amsterdam from 1978 to 1986 (housing, urban renewal, building control, land company). His are the winged words 'In gelul kan je niet wonen' (you can't live in hot air). He gave an enormous boost to urban renewal and housebuilding in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Jan Swammerdambrug
origins.en: Jan Swammerdam (1637-1680), anatomist and naturalist, who made important microscopic studies, preserved in his 'Bybel der natuure' (Bible of nature).

origins.name: Jan Wilsbrug
origins.en: Named after Jan Wils (1891-1972), architect of the Olympic Stadium and the two Citroën buildings on the Stadionplein. He also designed the City Theatre on the Kleine-Gartmanplantsoen.

origins.name: Joep Langebrug
origins.en: Joep Lange was a professor of infectious diseases and an AIDS expert, one of the most influential AIDS scientists in the world. He was killed on 17 July 2014 in the MH17 air disaster.

origins.name: Joes Kloppenburgbrug
origins.en: Joes Kloppenburg (1970-1996) was beaten to death by Richard L. on 17 August 1996 when he intervened in a street fight in the Voetboogsteeg with the words 'Kappen nou!' (stop it now!). This bridge is fairly close to where he died and is meant as a symbol against senseless violence.

origins.name: Johan Cruijffbrug
origins.en: Johan Cruijff, born 25 April 1947 in Amsterdam, died 24 March 2016 in Barcelona. Forward for Ajax 1964-1973.

origins.name: Johan Neeskensbrug
origins.en: Johan Neeskens, born 15 September 1951 in Heemstede. Midfielder for Ajax 1970-1974, with 124 league matches. Three times Dutch champion, three times KNVB Cup winner, three times winner of the European Cup, once winner of the Cup Winners' Cup, once winner of the Intercontinental Cup, twice winner of the European Super Cup; 49 caps and two World Cup finals. In 1969 Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final of the prestigious European Cup, today's Champions League. Ajax lost that final, but two years later, in 1971, won the most important prize in football after all. In the two following years Ajax retained the title, confirming itself as the standard-bearer of Dutch football.

origins.name: Johanna Borskibrug
origins.en: Johanna Borski (1764-1846) was called 'the financier of the Netherlands' because she invested in visionary projects such as De Nederlandsche Bank, the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij and the Hollandsche IJzeren Spoorweg-Maatschappij (railway company). She twice saved the Dutch state from bankruptcy. She was born Johanna van der Velde on the Vijzelstraat and had her office on the Keizersgracht near the Spiegelstraat. This bridge looks out on the building of the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij, which she helped found and twice saved from ruin.

origins.name: John Rädeckerbrug
origins.en: John Rädecker (1885-1956, born and died in Amsterdam) drew, painted, made prints and carved wooden sculptures. His first sculptures were of brick, such as the Worker for De Dageraad in Amsterdam. He became best known as designer of the sculptures on the National Monument on the Dam.

origins.name: Johnny & Jonesbrug
origins.en: Johnny & Jones was an Amsterdam jazz duo, in which Nol van Wesel (1918-1945) was Johnny and Max Kannewasser (1916-1945) Jones. Because they were Jewish they were interned in the Westerbork transit camp in 1943. Even so they managed to return briefly to Amsterdam to make some recordings, including the 'Westerbork Serenade'. On 4 September they were put on a transport to Germany, where they died of exhaustion in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp shortly before the liberation. Their most famous song was 'Meneer Dinges, weet niet wat swing is' (Mr Thingummy doesn't know what swing is).

origins.name: Kabouterbrug
origins.en: The Kabouterbrug is named after the Kabouter movement (1969-1974), a playful protest movement and local political party.

origins.name: Kadoelenbrug
origins.en: The name of the part of the municipality of Landsmeer that was added to Amsterdam on 1 August 1966. The name Kadoelen (or Quadolen) appears as early as 1375. In 1429 the manors of Landsmeer and Quadolen are mentioned, which then shared one lord. Old maps show Kadoelen as a hamlet along the Waterland sea dike (Landsmeerderdijk). The Kadoelenweg was taken over on 1 August 1966 under the name Zuideinde, but in 1970 that name was changed because of confusion with the Zuideinde (formerly Oostzaan).

origins.name: Kattenburgerbrug
origins.en: One of the three eastern islands, with Wittenburg and Oostenburg. It was already called Kattenburg before it was diked and built on in the second half of the seventeenth century. No explanation for the name has been found so far. There was a house called 'de Cat', but that name is only recorded in the eighteenth century. After many buildings had been demolished during the occupation, the rest were demolished in 1965-1968. Rebuilding then began on a new street plan. The Kattenburgerplein is the only thing that still recalls the old buildings.

origins.name: Kattenslootbrug
origins.en: The name of the ditch beneath it.

origins.name: Kees Fensbrug
origins.en: Kees Fens (1929-2008) was an Amsterdam literary critic, essayist and man of letters. He received the P.C. Hooft Prize in 1990 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Amsterdam in 2004. From his house he looked out on this bridge, and in 2008 he published the book 'Het geluk van de brug' (the happiness of the bridge).

origins.name: Keizersbrug
origins.en: It takes its name from the nearby Keizersstraat.

origins.name: Kinkerbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after Johannes Kinker (1764-1845), poet and lawyer in Amsterdam and The Hague, who later became a professor at Liège.

origins.name: Klimopbrug
origins.en: The climbing shrub (ivy).

origins.name: Koekjesbrug
origins.en: There are four possible explanations for the name of this fixed bridge. It may be named after a popular biscuit (koekjes) seller who was pushed into the mud here by jostling youths. There also used to be a small cocoa mill here where cocoa biscuits were sold. The name may also go back to the market gardener Pannenkoek, who once owned land next to the bridge. A fourth possibility is that it is named after a policeman called Koek, who just before the bridge opened walked across it demonstratively after a quarrel with the ferryman. The ferryman is then said to have written on the bridge railing 'Deze brug is gedoopt Koekjesbrug' (this bridge is christened Koekjesbrug).

origins.name: Kors van Bennekombrug
origins.en: Kors van Bennekom (Lodewijk, 13 July 1933 - Amsterdam, 4 October 2016) was an Amsterdam photographer and holder of the City of Amsterdam's Frans Banninck Cocq medal.

origins.name: Korte Ouderkerkerbrug
origins.en: Named after the village of Ouderkerk aan de Amstel, to which these roads lead. The prefix Korte (short) dates from 1956, after the dike was cut through for the industrial estate.

origins.name: Krijtbergbrug
origins.en: Named after the nearby Krijtberg, or St Francis Xavier church (sometimes also called the Rijtjeskerk), on the Singel. Consecrated in 1883, the church replaced the former clandestine church in the house de Crijtberg, served by the Jesuits.

origins.name: L.H. Sarlouisbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after Louis Hartog Sarlouis (1884-1942), founder of the Jewish secondary school (H.B.S.) and chief rabbi of Amsterdam from 1936 to 1942, the year he was deported to Auschwitz, where he died.

origins.name: Lau Mazirelbrug
origins.en: Laura Carola Mazirel (1907-1974), lawyer and solicitor in Amsterdam, who stood up for groups isolated in society: before the Second World War German refugees, after the war Gypsies and homosexuals. During the war she was involved both with the crèche of the Hollandsche Schouwburg, where the Jewish population was gathered before deportation, and with the resistance group around Gerrit van der Veen.

origins.name: Lee Millerbrug
origins.en: Lee Miller (1907-1977) was an American photographer and model, known as a war correspondent in the Second World War. She went on to become a renowned fashion and art photographer.

origins.name: Leeuwenputbrug
origins.en: In the first half of the seventeenth century the gallows field was embellished with a stone well with three tall columns topped by lions' heads, as though what took place there were a venerable ceremony. In time the remains of the bodies fell into the well. When the IJ froze over in winter, which then happened regularly, people crossed the ice on skates or sledges to take a look. The fun on the ice around the gallows well could take bizarre forms, as a print by Reinier Vinkeles from around 1780 shows. Close to the well stand two busy stalls selling snacks and hot drinks. A man relieves himself against the well, apparently to show his disgust.

origins.name: Leidsebrug
origins.en: The city of Leiden.

origins.name: Lex van Deldenbrug
origins.en: Alexander Zwaap (1919-1988), composer. Van Delden was the name he used from his time in hiding and in the resistance. In 1982 he received the City of Amsterdam's Pin of Merit.

origins.name: Liefdesbruggetje
origins.en: This bridge is called the Liefdesbruggetje (little bridge of love) because it is a favourite spot for wedding photos. From here you can look out over the park and the pond without seeing any buildings.

origins.name: Lijnbaansbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Lijnbaanssteeg, in which it lies. The alley dates from the fifteenth century, when the Singel was the outermost canal and the ropewalks (lijnbanen) of the ropemakers were here, on a kind of industrial estate.

origins.name: Lyceumbrug
origins.en: The name of this bridge refers to the nearby Amsterdams Lyceum (a secondary school).

origins.name: M. Justbrug
origins.en: Named after Chief Rabbi Meir Just (1908-2010), who served in Buitenveldert. He lived in Soetendael and so often walked over this bridge to the Jewish Cultural Centre on the Van der Boechorststraat.

origins.name: M.S. Vaz Diasbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after Mozes Salomon Vaz Dias (1882-1963), founder of the press agency M.S. Vaz Dias, which in 1934 merged into the Algemeen Nederlands Persbureau (ANP), which he co-founded.

origins.name: Machineslootbrug
origins.en: This bridge keeps alive the memory of one of the former names of today's Admiralengracht.

origins.name: Madibabrug
origins.en: Nickname of Nelson Mandela.

origins.name: Magere Brug
origins.en: Around 1670 a drawbridge was laid over the Amstel so narrow that it was only fit for pedestrians. Although officially called the Kerkstraatbrug (after the Lange Kerkstraat), people stubbornly called it the 'Magere brug' (skinny bridge), and the city council then adopted the name. The story of the Mager sisters, who lived nearby, belongs to the realm of fables. Old pictures show that the old bridge was a simple wooden structure: the deck of the fixed part lay on simple wooden trestles, while the movable middle was a drawbridge with a single leaf. In 1772 it was given a double leaf, and in 1871 the bridge was demolished entirely and replaced by one with nine spans.

origins.name: Majoor Bosshardtbrug
origins.en: Alida Margaretha Bosshardt (1913-2007) became known for her work for the Salvation Army, most of which took place right around this bridge. Here on the Wallen she also founded the Goodwill Centre. In 2009 she was voted 'Greatest Amsterdammer of all time'. The 'Major' (who was actually a lieutenant-colonel) was a true bridge-builder between different groups, which is why a bridge was chosen for her rather than a street.

origins.name: Margaret Bourke-Whitebrug
origins.en: Margaret Bourke-White (1904-1971) was the first war correspondent accredited to the US Army and a photographer for the US Air Force.

origins.name: Mariniersbrug
origins.en: After the nearby Marines barracks.

origins.name: Marten Toonderbrug
origins.en: Marten Toonder (Rotterdam, 2 May 1912 - Laren, 27 July 2005) was a Dutch comics author. Besides his great role in literature, Toonder also put his talents to use during the Second World War.

origins.name: Meerbrug
origins.en: The name of this fixed bridge in Kadoelen is derived from the surrounding hamlet called 't Meertje, which belonged to Landsmeer before the annexation of 1921.

origins.name: Mien Ruysbrug
origins.en: Wilhelmina Jacoba (Mien) Moussault-Ruys, better known by her maiden name as Mien Ruys (Dedemsvaart, April 12, 1904 - Deventer, January 9, 1999), was an internationally known Dutch garden architect. In the Netherlands, she was nicknamed Bielzen Mien because she was the pioneer in the use of railway bogies in gardens, something that was particularly popular in the 1970s. She liked to work with straight shapes: rectangles, squares and clear lines. She was one of the first in the Netherlands to seriously deal with smaller city gardens as a garden architect.

origins.name: Muiderbergbrug
origins.en: Named after the town of Muiderberg

origins.name: Muntsluis
origins.en: The Amsterdammers simply call it the Mint. In the building next to the Mint Tower (remnant of the Regulierspoort), coins were minted for a period of time in the seventeenth century. Since then, the name Mint has been associated with it.

origins.name: Nesciobrug
origins.en: Nescio was the pseudonym of the Amsterdam writer J.H.F. Grönloh, known for novellas such as De Uitvreter and Titaantjes. He enjoyed walking in the area around the neighboring Diemerzeedijk and the Buiten-IJ.

origins.name: Nieuwe Amstelbrug
origins.en: When this double bascule bridge, designed partly by Berlage, opened in 1903, it was the newest bridge over the Amstel. The Hoge Sluis was also known as the Amstel Bridge, but this bridge was newer, hence the Nieuwe Amstelbrug

origins.name: Nieuwe-Wercksbrug
origins.en: Named after the original name for the current Jordaan.

origins.name: NSM-brug
origins.en: refers to the Nederlandsche Scheepsbouw Maatschappij, which was here until 1946. After merging with the NSM, it continued as NDSM with the Nederderlandsche Dok Maatschappij (NDM).

origins.name: Oetewalerbrug
origins.en: bridge from 1924 is named after the village of Oetewaal, or Outewaal or Houtewaal, which used to be located on the Zeedijk near the current Muiderpoort. The village, which was already mentioned in 1387, was burned down by the Spanish in 1575 and devastated by a storm surge in 1651, but rebuilt again and again. In 1658 it was annexed by the municipality of Amsterdam. Linnaeusstraat was called Oetewalerweg before 1878 and was the road from Oetewaal to Watergraafsmeer De Oetewalerbrug is also popularly known as Hemabrug due to the proximity of the Hema

origins.name: Omvalbrug
origins.en: Landtong between the Amstel and the ring canal of the Watergraafsmeer. Since the seventeenth century or earlier so named after a 'wreck' located there, that is, a construction site or ruin. The name has been passed down with the transition on 1-1-1921 of this part of the municipality of Ouder-Amstel.

origins.name: Oost-Indische Huisbrug
origins.en: Named after the nearby Oost-Indische House on the Kloveniersburgwal corner of Oude Hoogstraat

origins.name: Oosterbeerbrug
origins.en: Oosterbeer is a former stronghold, on which the De Gooyer mill stood for a while.

origins.name: Osdorperwegbrug
origins.en: Named after the neighborhood of Osdorp. On old maps, this neighborhood is mentioned as Oostdorp. In 1957, construction began on the garden city of Osdorp, which was practically completed in 1973. The Osdorperweg used to bear the names Herenstraat (in the village of Sloten) and Slimmeweg.

origins.name: Oude Haagsebrug
origins.en: This bridge, which is currently in use as a bus lane, is named after the road it lies on. This road used to lead to The Hague as part of the former Rijksweg 4. Now that this has not been the case since 1966, this road is called the Oude Haagsweg.

origins.name: Oude Kinkerbrug
origins.en: Johannes Kinker (1764-1845) was a Dutch poet, philosopher and lawyer

origins.name: Overschiebrug-Noord
origins.en: The former village in South Holland, part of Rotterdam since 1941.

origins.name: Overschiebrug-Zuid
origins.en: The former village in Zuid-Holland, since 1941 part of Rotterdam.

origins.name: Paleis voor Volksvlijtbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Paleis for Volksvlijt, which was burned down in 1929 and stood where the current Nederlandsche Bank is located.

origins.name: Pastoorsbrug
origins.en: The derivation of the name of this fixed bridge is not known with certainty. Perhaps the former Roman Catholic secret church 'De Zaaier', which was located at Keizersgracht 22, has something to do with this bridge name.

origins.name: Pelikaanbrug
origins.en: Given the proximity of the d'Peliekaan warehouse at Hoogte Kadijk 51

origins.name: Peter Postbrug
origins.en: Peter Post (1933-2011) In 1949, this Amsterdam native won his first cycling championship at the Amsterdam Slagersjongens and then he would grow up as a track cyclist to become the undisputed 'Emperor of the Six Days'. As a road cyclist, he won Paris-Roubaix in 1964. As team manager, he led Joop Zoetemelk to the final victory in the Tour de France in 1980.

origins.name: Pia Beckbrug
origins.en: Pieternella (Pia) Beck (1926 - 2009) was a Dutch jazz pianist. She was named the best jazz pianist in the world by her colleague Oscar Peterson. She was one of the first artists to openly come out as lesbian. In the Park Haagseweg, all the streets are named after famous jazz musicians.

origins.name: Piet Bakkerbrug
origins.en: Piet Bakker was a writer and journalist. In addition to his love for the Pijp, Piet Bakker also expressed his love for Amsterdam in books such as 'Amsterdam as it lives and works' from 1933 and 'Guide to Amsterdam' from 1937. But he has given Amsterdam above all its most iconic 'darling' in the person of Ciske de Rat, to whom two successful films and a musical are dedicated. In the vicinity

origins.name: Piet Keizerbrug
origins.en: Piet Keizer born June 14, 1943 in Amsterdam / died February 10, 2017 in Amsterdam. Striker Ajax 1961 - 1974 365 matches in Eredivisie (146 goals) 6 x national champion / 5 winner x KNVB Cup / 3 x winner European Cup for national champions / 2 x winner European Supercup/ 1 x winner Intertoto cup / 1 winner world cup. Piet Keizer played 34 international matches and never played for a club other than Ajax. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final of the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final, but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Piet Meerburgbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after Piet Meerburg, who was born in De Bilt in 1919 and died in Amsterdam in 2010. He was involved in saving Jewish children during World War II, for which he received the Yad Vashem award. One of those children was the later mayor Ed van Thijn. He was also a prominent theater entrepreneur in Amsterdam. For example, he was director of the Nieuwe de la Mar theater for many years and produced the musical My Fair Lady.

origins.name: Pieter Goemansbrug
origins.en: Pieter Goemans (Peter Shott), who lived from 1925 to 2000 in the 1950s, found inspiration for his song 'Aan de Amsterdamse grachten' on this fixed bridge. A plaque on this bridge reminds us of this.

origins.name: Raampoort
origins.en: This bridge is named after the Raampoort, which was demolished in 1844

origins.name: Reesluis
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Reestraat, in which it lies.

origins.name: Rie Beisenherzbrug
origins.en: Maria Martha (Rie) Beisenherz (Amsterdam, September 8, 1901 – Bussum, April 12, 1992) She was a Dutch swimmer. She was a pioneer in women's swimming. When she wanted to join the swimming club HDZ as a thirteen-year-old, she was rejected because she was considered too young. Therefore, she, along with a number of other swimmers, founded the Amsterdamsche Dames Zwemclub (ADZ). Beisenherz represented the Netherlands once at the Olympic Games: 'Antwerp 1920'. She was the Netherlands' first female participant in the modern Olympic Games ever. She competed in the 100 meters freestyle and reached the semifinals in Antwerp in this event, with a time of 1.22.6.

origins.name: Rotterdammerbrug
origins.en: Named after the city of Rotterdam

origins.name: Rozenoordmetrobrug
origins.en: Former nursery on the Amstel, located between Zorgvlied and the Kalfje. Also the location of the boat connection between Ouderkerk and Amsterdam.

origins.name: Rozenoordspoorbrug
origins.en: Former nursery on the Amstel, located between Zorgvlied and the Kalfje. Also the location of the boat connection between Ouderkerk and Amsterdam.

origins.name: Ruud Krolbrug
origins.en: Ruud Krol born March 24, 1949 in Amsterdam, 6 x national champion / 4 winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner Europa Cup National Champions / 2 winner European Supercup / 1 winner Intercontinental Cup (Wereldbeker). Krol played 339 competitive matches for Ajax. He played 83 international matches. Played 2 World Cup finals, including 1 as captain of the Netherlands. Was assistant coach at Ajax between 2002 and 2005. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Schellingwouderbrug
origins.en: Village Schellingwoude

origins.name: Schollenbrug
origins.en: Named after the roadside inn that used to stand here, and which took its name from the old Schollenbrug on the Weesperzijde, connecting the Watergraafsmeer to the city. That bridge was previously called Schulpbrug, after the 17th-century inn the Schulp. This was on the other side of the bridge, so in the Watergraafsmeer (with a shell or shell in the facade).

origins.name: Sint Nicolaasbrug
origins.en: Saint Nicholas of Myra is the patron saint of Amsterdam and this bridge is opposite the Basilica of Saint Nicholas from 1887 on Prins Hendrikkade.

origins.name: Sloterdijkerbrug
origins.en: The old dike village, of which only the church and a small part remain today. It belonged to the municipality of Sloten, which was annexed to Amsterdam in 1921. The village was originally called Sloterdam and had a harbor and a lock in earlier centuries.

origins.name: Solitudobrug
origins.en: The name is based on former country estates along the Amstel and in the Watergraafsmeer.

origins.name: Solitudolaanspoorbrug
origins.en: Former country house near the Amstel and the Weespertrekvaart, which was located approximately at this location. It was already mentioned in 1730, and still existed in 1798.

origins.name: Staalmeestersbrug
origins.en: In the Staalstraat was the Staalhof, where the Staalmasters worked, who were made famous by Rembrandt.

origins.name: Staatsliedenbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after the neighborhood in which it is located, the Staatsliedenbuurt

origins.name: Steenhouwerijbrug
origins.en: Named after the stonemasons who worked in the Stads Metseltuin on the Leidsegracht.

origins.name: Tante Saarbrug
origins.en: Sara Bacharach, better known as Aunt Saar, honorary citizen of Amsterdam, sold flowers on Rembrandtplein for more than 60 years, and had her storage on Torbeckeplein. She was a well-known figure in Amsterdam. In bitter poverty, she earned a living for her family of 9 children by selling flowers. In the early morning, she would take a train to the auction in Aalsmeer to buy flowers. First she walked around the city with a basket, later she had a stall on Rembrandtplein. She survived several concentration camps, lost 3 children and 6 grandchildren, but she was a very strong woman, and there is also a lot known about her in the archives of Amsterdam. She was born in 1887 and died in 1982. She came from the old Jewish working class, a hard-working woman and a true Amsterdammer.

origins.name: Tetje de Jongbrug
origins.en: Theodora (Tetje) de Jong (Uithoorn, May 2, 1918 - Drachten, January 21, 1999) was the first paid female police commissioner in the Netherlands. In 1954, the same year in which the first women joined the uniform service at the Amsterdam police, De Jong was appointed chief inspector. On January 1, 1964, De Jong was officially appointed police commissioner in Amsterdam. In 1977, De Jong received a Royal award due to her great significance for the Amsterdam police: she was appointed Officer of the Order of Orange-Nassau.

origins.name: Theo Fransmanbrug
origins.en: Theo Frenchman, who was the first district chairman of Amsterdam-North from 1981 to 1990. He worked as such to find new destinations for the NDSM site after the closure of the shipyard.

origins.name: Tijnmuidenbrug
origins.en: The English port town of Tynemouth, near Newcastle, according to a spelling as it appears on Dutch sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Timo Smeehuijzenbrug
origins.en: Timo Smeehuijzen was a 20-year-old soldier who died in Afghanistan on June 15, 2007. Before that, he attended school at the nearby Fons Vitae high school, hence this location. This bridge is also a tribute to all other soldiers who died in Afghanistan.

origins.name: Torensluis
origins.en: The name of this fixed bridge refers to the Jan Roodenpoortstoren, which used to stand next to the gate in the city wall here and was demolished in 1829. The base of the tower is still located on the side of this bridge.

origins.name: Torontobrug
origins.en: This double bascule bridge is named after the city of Toronto in Canada, a sister city of Amsterdam. On October 2, 1974, a plaque was unveiled here by Mayor David Crombie of Toronto to strengthen this sister city relationship. Toronto therefore also has an Amsterdam Bridge.

origins.name: Tulpbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after Nicolaas Tulp (1593-1674), professor at the Athenaeum Illustre for the surgical guild. He was also mayor of Amsterdam several times, but he is best known for his anatomical lecture, which was immortalized by Rembrandt.

origins.name: Utrechtsebrug
origins.en: Named after the city of Utrecht.

origins.name: Van Mierlobrug
origins.en: Henricus Antonius Franciscus Maria Oliva (Hans) van Mierlo (Breda, August 18, 1931 - Amsterdam, March 11, 2010) Dutch journalist and politician. In 1966, together with Hans Gruijters, he was the main initiator of the establishment of the social liberal party Democrats '66. For this party, he served as political leader for two separate periods and was a member of both the House of Representatives and the Senate (Eerste Kamer). In the 1980s, he was also Minister of Defense in the Van Agt II and III cabinets and from 1994 to 1998, he was Minister of Foreign Affairs and Vice Prime Minister in the 'purple' Kok I cabinet, which was partly due to him.

origins.name: Varkenssluis
origins.en: This bridge is named after the pig market, which was held here in the sixteenth century

origins.name: Veebrug
origins.en: Named after the former Veemarkt

origins.name: Veenderijbrug
origins.en: This bridge came into existence around 1919 as a lift bridge over the Scheisloot. It was used for digging the peat out of the Osdorper Binnenpolder when the drainage channel (tocht) behind the Osdorperweg was also widened to Osdorpervaart to allow the peat ships to enter the area as far as possible.

origins.name: Volewijckbrug
origins.en: This bridge is named after De Volewijck, a bird-rich peninsula in the IJ, over which the city gained control in 1393. On this land stood a mass grave with stakes until 1795, on which the bodies of criminals, who had been hanged on the Dam,

origins.name: Vondelbrug
origins.en: Joost van den Vondel (1587-1679) was a poet who wrote many tragic plays, the most famous of which is 'Gijsbrecht van Aemstel'.

origins.name: Waalseilandbrug
origins.en: Named after the word 'waal' which means a piece of water surrounded by rows of poles in which ships could overwinter or be repaired

origins.name: Walenweeshuissluis
origins.en: The Walenweeshuis on the corner of the Vijzelgracht was built in 1669-1671 by Adriaan Dortsman and was intended for the orphans of the French or Walloon church.

origins.name: Warmoesbrug
origins.en: Named after the former Warmoesgracht, which was filled in for the construction of Raadhuisstraat.

origins.name: Wasknijper
origins.en: This lifting bridge owes its name to the design of the counterweights on the lever that resembles a pair of pliers.

origins.name: West-Indische Huisbrug
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the neighboring West-Indische House.

origins.name: Westerdoksdijkspoorbrug
origins.en: The causeway, built between 1830 and 1834, which formed the Nieuwe Waal into the Westerdok. When the railway was extended to Stationseiland at the end of the late 1880s of the nineteenth century, a section of the dock had to be filled in and the Westerdokskade was built. The Westerdokstraat was laid out and named in 1879, but disappeared in 1973 due to the widening of the Haarlemmer Houttuinen.

origins.name: Westerdoksluis
origins.en: The causeway, built between 1830 and 1834, which formed the Nieuwe Waal into the Westerdok. When the railway was extended to Stationseiland at the end of the late 1880s of the nineteenth century, a section of the dock had to be filled in and the Westerdokskade was built. The Westerdokstraat was laid out and named in 1879, but disappeared in 1973 due to the widening of the Haarlemmer Houttuinen.

origins.name: Westerkeersluis
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after the Westerkanaal, over which it lies, and because it is located in the western part of Amsterdam.

origins.name: Weteringpoort
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Weteringpoort, which stood nearby here from 1688 to 1841. The name recalls the Wetering, which used to enter the city from Kalfjeslaan here and flowed into the Spui. The current Boerenwetering is still a remnant here.

origins.name: Wiegbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after the type of bridge it originally represented. A wiegbrug (rocking bridge) is a rolling bascule bridge.

origins.name: Wil de Graaffbrug
origins.en: Wil de Graaff (1928-2001) served on the municipal council of Bos en Lommer from 1990 until his death. First for the CPN and from 1994 for Bewonersbelangen Bos en Lommer, of which he was the founder. In 2001 he received the gold medal of merit of the city of Amsterdam for his more than 30 years of commitment to the interests of tenants in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Willemsbrug
origins.en: This bascule bridge is named after King William I (1772-1843), who opened the nearby Willemspoort in 1840

origins.name: Wim Sonneveldbrug
origins.en: Wim Sonneveld (1917-1974) was a Dutch cabaretier and singer, who is considered together with Wim Kan and Toon Hermans as one of the 'Big three of Dutch cabaret'. He gave great fame to the song 'Aan de Amsterdamse grachten', which was written in the 1950s by Pieter Goemans on the nearby bridge 93 over the Leidsegracht. He was associated with the then Nieuwe De la Martheater, which is located near this bridge, from 1952 until his death. In the current De la Martheater, there is a hall named after him

origins.name: Wim Suurbierbrug
origins.en: Wim Suurbier, born 16-1-1945 in Eindhoven, right back, from 1964 to 1977 Ajax played 392 matches in the Eredivisie 7 x national champion / 5 winner KNVB Cup / 3 x winner European Cup / 2 x winner European Super Cup/ 1 x winner Intercontinental Cup (Wereldbeker) 60 x international, played 2 World Cup finals, not born but raised in Amsterdam. In 1969, Ajax became the first Dutch club to reach the final in the prestigious Europa Cup for Landskampioenen. Today, that tournament continues under the name 'Champions League'. Ajax lost that final but two years later, in 1971, Ajax still won the most important football prize.

origins.name: Witte Boogbrug
origins.en: Named after her appearance, it is a white arch bridge

origins.name: Yaa Adu-Ampomabrug
origins.en: Nana Yaa Adu-Ampoma (1959 - 2000) was a municipal council member in Zuidoost. Nana Yaa Adu-Ampoma has made several important contributions to the immigrant community in the Netherlands, including the Ghanaian-Dutch community.

origins.name: Zaagpoort
origins.en: This fixed bridge is named after the Sawmill Gate, which was demolished in 1844. This gate was in turn named after the many sawmills, which stood here until the end of the nineteenth century.

origins.name: Zebrabrug
origins.en: Named after the zebra species

origins.name: Zeeburgerbrug
origins.en: The fortress 'Seeburgh', which stood halfway through the seventeenth century at the end of the dike. The Zeeburgerdijk is a part of the original sea dike of the North Sea. Before the Watergraafsmeer was drained, this was the only connection in the direction of Naarden.

origins.name: 's-Gravelandse Veer
origins.en: The quay used to be the mooring place of the scheduled passenger barges (beurtschepen) to this village in Het Gooi, where a number of Amsterdam regent families had their country residences. Before 1913 the quay was called Binnen-Amstel.

origins.name: 's-Gravendijkdreef
origins.en: Name of a farm in Noordwijkerhout (Zuid-Holland).

origins.name: 's-Gravenhekje
origins.en: Until the eighteenth century this was a timber storage yard. According to a bylaw (keur) of 1663, this timber yard could only be closed off with a hek (gate). It is assumed that a timber merchant named De Graaf had his timber yard here, hence De Graafs hek and later 's-Gravenhek. The name first appears towards the end of the eighteenth century.

origins.name: 's-Gravesandeplein
origins.en: Willem Jan van 's-Gravesande (1688-1742), professor of mathematics and astronomy at Leiden. He was the first follower of Newton in the Netherlands.

origins.name: 's-Gravesandestraat
origins.en: Willem Jan van 's-Gravesande (1688-1742), professor of mathematics and astronomy at Leiden. He was the first follower of Newton in the Netherlands.

origins.name: 't Kleine Loopveld
origins.en: The name recalls the history of Amstelland. In the sixteenth century many inhabitants of the area made their living by dredging. Dredging up the deep peat layer created large lakes, between which strips of land called loopvelden (walking fields) were left so that people could get from one village to another. One of these was the Kleine Loopveld, which was later called Kalfjeslaan. The name has now been given to a strip of parkland. The Grote Loopveld is now the Ouderkerkerlaan in Amstelveen.

origins.name: 't Nopeind
origins.en: Old local name, formed by contraction and corruption of 'op 't einde' (at the end).

origins.name: 't Voorwerf
origins.en: Old local name. Werf (yard) is used to denote a site where work is carried out.

origins.name: 1e Glanshof
origins.en: The name belongs to the theme 'Sociaal en tevreden wonen' (Social and contented living) for the G-buurt Grunder/Grubbehoeve.

origins.name: 1e Kekerstraat
origins.en: A legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is borrowed from the Latin cicer(a), meaning 'grey pea'. Because the vowel was shortened, keker came to sound like kikker. A kikkererwt (chickpea) is therefore really a 'pea pea'.

origins.name: 2e Glanshof
origins.en: The name belongs to the theme 'Sociaal en tevreden wonen' (Social and contented living) for the G-buurt Grunder/Grubbehoeve.

origins.name: 2e Kekerstraat
origins.en: A legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is borrowed from the Latin cicer(a), meaning 'grey pea'. Because the vowel was shortened, keker came to sound like kikker. A kikkererwt (chickpea) is therefore really a 'pea pea'.

origins.name: 3e Kekerstraat
origins.en: A legume. The Middle Dutch word keker is borrowed from the Latin cicer(a), meaning 'grey pea'. Because the vowel was shortened, keker came to sound like kikker. A kikkererwt (chickpea) is therefore really a 'pea pea'.

origins.name: A. Eversplein
origins.en: Adriaan Evers (1914-1997), architect. Together with Geert Sarlemijn he designed churches, schools and housing. He was an exponent of the conservative Bossche School, which is associated with Catholicism.

origins.name: A. Moenstraat
origins.en: Adriaan Moen (1879-1950), Amsterdam architect. He designed various factory buildings, villas and shops in the style of the Amsterdamse School. He built the Betlehemkerk on the Zwanenplein.

origins.name: A. Reitsmakade
origins.en: Auguste Chrétien Joseph Reitsma (1922-1943), resistance fighter. He worked for the underground press and was one of the nine people involved in the attack on the Amsterdam population registry (Amsterdams Bevolkingsregister) on 27 March 1943. He was executed by firing squad in Overveen on 1 July 1943.

origins.name: A.A. de Lannoy-Willemsstraat
origins.en: Angela Altagracia de Lannoy-Willems (1913-1983), born on Curaçao. From the founding of the Nationale Volkspartij onwards, she was active in the party's women's section. In 1949 she became the first woman to be sworn in as a member of the Staten van de Nederlandse Antillen, and in 1951 she was also elected a member of the Eilandsraad van Curaçao.

origins.name: A.J. Koejemansstraat
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1903-1982), editor-in-chief of the underground newspaper 'De Waarheid' (The Truth). He worked for broad cooperation within the resistance.

origins.name: A.J. Krophollerstraat
origins.en: Alexander Jacobus Kropholler (1881-1973), architect. He mainly built churches and town halls, and was known for his brickwork, sturdy furniture, heavy doors and generous timber roofs.

origins.name: A.M. de Jongstraat
origins.en: Adrianus M. de Jong (1888-1943), novelist, murdered by the occupiers in his home in Blaricum. He is best known for his Merijntje Gijzen cycle.

origins.name: A.S. Onderwijzerhof
origins.en: Abraham Samson Onderwijzer (1862-1934), rabbi from 1888 and chief rabbi of the Joodse Gemeente Amsterdam (Jewish Community of Amsterdam) from 1917. The courtyard was laid out on a site behind three former synagogues (since 1987 the Joods Historisch Museum).

origins.name: Aaf Bouberstraat
origins.en: Aafje ten Hoope (1885-1974), actress, wife of Herman Bouber. She started out in 1911 with Colnot and Poons, and from 1920 she and her husband ran their own company: Het Volkstoneel. She acted in 'De Jantjes' and in 'Op hoop van Zegen'.

origins.name: Aagtdorperpad
origins.en: Village in Noord-Holland, part of the municipality of Schoorl.

origins.name: Aakhof
origins.en: An aak is a flat-bottomed inland vessel.

origins.name: Aakstraat
origins.en: An aak is a flat-bottomed inland vessel.

origins.name: Aalbersestraat
origins.en: Petrus Josephus Mattheus Aalberse (1871-1948). Roman Catholic politician and statesman, professor at Delft. Minister of Labour, Commerce and Industry from 1918 to 1925.

origins.name: Aalsmeerplein
origins.en: Town in Noord-Holland, the largest flower centre in Europe.

origins.name: Aalsmeerweg
origins.en: Town in Noord-Holland, the largest flower centre in Europe.

origins.name: Aambeeldstraat
origins.en: An aambeeld (anvil) is a blacksmith's tool: an iron block for forging on. Before 1948 the street was part of the Schaafstraat.

origins.name: Aandammerbrug
origins.en: The Aandammerbrug is named after the Aandammergouw, in which it lies, seen from the municipality of Broek in Waterland. The Aandammerbrug is one of the smallest bridges in Amsterdam; it was originally a wooden bridge built on six trestles. It was replaced by a so-called hoge zijl (high sluice).

origins.name: Aandewind
origins.en: A term for a position in sailing.

origins.name: Aardbeistraat
origins.en: Named after the strawberry, a fruit.

origins.name: Aaron Coplandstraat
origins.en: American composer (1900-1990). He composed symphonies, ballets, film music and an opera ('The tender land'). He promoted American music through publicity and lectures.

origins.name: Aart van der Leeuwstraat
origins.en: Writer (1876-1931), author of sketches, stories and rural idylls.

origins.name: Abbenesstraat
origins.en: Village in the Haarlemmermeer.

origins.name: Abberdaan
origins.en: The Scottish port of Aberdeen, in a spelling found on Dutch sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Abcouderpad
origins.en: Name of the underlying path.

origins.name: Abcouderstraatweg
origins.en: The road leads to the village of Abcoude (Utrecht). Before the motorway was built, it was the route between Amsterdam and Utrecht.

origins.name: Abe Lenstralaan
origins.en: Frisian footballer (1920-1985). At fifteen he made his debut in Heerenveen's first team. At nineteen he played for the Dutch national team for the first time, and he went on to play for it 47 times in all. He scored 33 goals for Oranje in total, as many as Johan Cruijff later did. In 1951 Lenstra was chosen as the first Sportsman of the Year.

origins.name: Abebe Bikilalaan
origins.en: Ethiopian athlete who won gold in the marathon at the 1960 Olympic Games in Rome. He became a legend because he ran it barefoot. In 1964 he won gold again, this time not barefoot.

origins.name: Abidjanweg
origins.en: African port city in Ivory Coast. The street lies near the Afrikahaven in the western port area.

origins.name: Abraham de Haanstraat
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1910-1945) who was part of a resistance group within the Kromhout Motorenfabriek, where he worked. After the February Strike of 1941 he was arrested and released, and in 1942 he was arrested again on suspicion of illegal activities. He died in Bergen-Belsen on 10 May 1945.

origins.name: Abraham Kuyperplein
origins.en: Minister (clergyman), politician and statesman (1837-1920). He promoted anti-revolutionary principles in church and society. He succeeded Groen van Prinsterer as leader of the Anti-Revolutionaire Partij (Anti-Revolutionary Party) and founded the Vrije Universiteit in 1880. In 1888, together with the Roman Catholic statesman Dr Schaepman, he forged the alliance between Rome and Dordt, which led to the first coalition cabinet (1888-1891). He was Prime Minister from 1901 to 1905.

origins.name: Abraham Kuyperstraat
origins.en: Minister (clergyman), politician and statesman (1837-1920). He promoted anti-revolutionary principles in church and society. He succeeded Groen van Prinsterer as leader of the Anti-Revolutionaire Partij (Anti-Revolutionary Party) and founded the Vrije Universiteit in 1880. In 1888, together with the Roman Catholic statesman Dr Schaepman, he forged the alliance between Rome and Dordt, which led to the first coalition cabinet (1888-1891). He was Prime Minister from 1901 to 1905.

origins.name: Abram Dudok van Heelstraat
origins.en: Abraham Everardus Dudok van Heel (1802-1893), who in 1827, together with Paul van Vlissingen, founded the company that later grew into Werkspoor.

origins.name: Abrikozenstraat
origins.en: Named after the apricot, a fruit.

origins.name: Abtswoudepad
origins.en: Named after the village of the same name near Delft (Zuid-Holland). It was named in 1959 with the suffix 'straat' (street); because the urban layout was changed, this was altered to 'pad' (path) in 1967.

origins.name: Accason
origins.en: A corrupted spelling of the French port of Archachon, as it appears on sea charts from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

origins.name: Accraweg
origins.en: African port city, capital of Ghana. The street lies near the Afrikahaven in the western port area.

origins.name: Accumulatorweg
origins.en: A device for storing electrical energy (in Dutch usually shortened to accu).

origins.name: Achillesstraat
origins.en: The Greek hero who fell in the Trojan War (1195 to 1184 BC) when he was struck in his most vulnerable spot, his heel (the Achilles tendon).

origins.name: Achter Oosteinde
origins.en: Named after its location: behind (achter) the Oosteinde.

origins.name: Achterdek
origins.en: Achterdek (afterdeck): one of the decks of a ship.

origins.name: Achtergouwtje
origins.en: Named after its location relative to the village centre. Gouw is the Waterland word for a village road.

origins.name: Achtergracht
origins.en: This canal was dug around 1660 behind (achter) the four main canals, hence the name. It connected the Reguliersgracht with the Amstel. In 1870 most of it was filled in.

origins.name: Achterlaan
origins.en: Named after its location in relation to the village centre.

origins.name: Achtersteven
origins.en: Part of a ship's hull: the achtersteven is the stern.

origins.name: Ad Windighof
origins.en: Important photojournalist (1912-1996). During the Second World War he belonged to the group of photographers later known as 'De Ondergedoken Camera' (The Hidden Camera), which clandestinely documented the resistance and the Hunger Winter. After the war he was a co-founder of the photographers' association GKf.

origins.name: Adam Smithplein
origins.en: Scottish economist (1723-1790), founder of classical liberalism. Smith believed that the pursuit of individual self-interest would produce the greatest benefit for society. A free market would yield the most for society as a whole. In his most important work, 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' of 1776, he laid the foundations of modern capitalism.

origins.name: Adam van Germezhof
origins.en: Actor from the time of Vondel (1610-1667). He played roles in the plays of Brederode.

origins.name: Adama van Scheltemaplein
origins.en: Carel Steven Adama van Scheltema (1877-1924), socialist poet, popular for his simplicity and clarity.

origins.name: Adamello
origins.en: Mountain peak in Italy, 3554 metres high.

origins.name: Adelaarsweg
origins.en: The bird of prey (an adelaar is an eagle). Originally this road began at the IJ, where the 'Adelaarswegpont' ferry landed and where, until 1956, the station building of the tram to Purmerend and Edam stood. That section is now part of the Meeuwenlaan.

origins.name: Adèle Opzoomerstraat
origins.en: Writer (1857-1925) who wrote historical novels under the pseudonym A.S.L. Wallis.

origins.name: Adingerdorphof
origins.en: A village near Medemblik that was drowned in the fifteenth century.

origins.name: Admiraal De Ruijterweg
origins.en: Michiel Adriaansz. de Ruyter (1607-1676), the renowned admiral of Holland and West Friesland. He was born in Vlissingen. In Amsterdam he lived on what is now the Prins Hendrikkade.

origins.name: Admiraal Helfrichstraat
origins.en: Conrad E.L. Helfrich (1886-1962), fleet commander and commander-in-chief of the Allied naval forces in the South-West Pacific (1942).

origins.name: Admiralengracht
origins.en: A collective name for the admirals from Holland and Zeeland after whom the streets in the surrounding neighbourhood are named.

origins.name: Admiraliteitstraat
origins.en: In the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands there were five boards of supreme commanders for naval affairs (admiralties), one of which was in Amsterdam.

origins.name: Adolf van Nassaustraat
origins.en: The younger brother (1540-1568) of Prince William of Orange. He was killed in the Battle of Heiligerlee against the Spaniards.

origins.name: Adolphine Eduardine Kokplantsoen
origins.en: Lawyer (1879-1928). In 1900 she began studying law, and three years later she became the first Dutch woman to be sworn in as a lawyer. She campaigned above all for improving women's right to a say in decisions and their legal capacity.

origins.name: Adriaan Ditvoorsthof
origins.en: Film director (1940-1987). With his dark, bizarre and lyrical films and his new ideas about film grammar and camerawork, he became the figurehead of Dutch experimental avant-garde cinema.

origins.name: Adriaan Dorsmanstraat
origins.en: Master builder (1638-1682). His works include the Ronde Lutherse kerk (1668) and the Oosterkerk (1669).

origins.name: Adriaan Kluitstraat
origins.en: Historian (1735-1807) and professor at Leiden. A specialist in the Middle Ages.

origins.name: Adriaan Loosjesstraat
origins.en: Teacher of the Mennonite congregation at Westzaandam (1689-1767), known for his 'Beschrijving van de Zaanlandse dorpen' (Description of the Zaan villages).

origins.name: Adriaan van Bergenstraat
origins.en: The Brabant peat skipper who in 1590 smuggled Sea Beggars into Breda in his peat boat.

origins.name: Adriaan van der Horststraat
origins.en: Actor, director and theatre manager (1868-1942). He staged the plays of Herman Heijermans. His wife, Wilhelmina van der Horst-van der Lugt Melsert, was a great tragedienne.

origins.name: Adriaan van Oordthof
origins.en: Writer (1865-1910) who belonged to the school of the Tachtigers (the Movement of the Eighties) (1865-1910). He wrote historical novels.

origins.name: Adrianus van Waertweg
origins.en: Resistance fighter (1915-1942) who took part in underground work in Amsterdam Noord, including distributing 'De Waarheid' and pamphlets aimed at the German occupier. He was arrested in 1941 and died a year later, on 9 June, in a prison.

origins.name: Adrichemstraat
origins.en: Former settlement in the Noordzeekanaal area, east of Beverwijk.

origins.name: Adriënne Solserhof
origins.en: Variety artiste (1873-1943) from the Jordaan who enjoyed great success in theatre and cinema in the 1920s.

origins.name: Aert van Nesstraat
origins.en: Naval captain (1625-1693), vice-admiral under Michiel de Ruyter from 1666. He took part in the expedition to Chatham and fought in the naval battles of Solebay and Kijkduin.

origins.name: Afrikanerplein
origins.en: The usual term for white people born in South Africa. The square lies in the district where the names recall the struggle of the Dutch Boers, first against the indigenous population and later against the English.

origins.name: Afroditekade
origins.en: Figure from Greek mythology, goddess of love, fertility and beauty. Her equivalent in Roman mythology is Venus.

origins.name: Agamemnonstraat
origins.en: The legendary figure who led the Greeks against Troy in the Trojan War (1195 to 1184 BC).

origins.name: Agatha Christiesingel
origins.en: Agatha Mary Clarisse Miller (1891-1976), British writer of detective novels and stories. (Christie is the surname of her first husband.)

origins.name: Agatha Dekenstraat
origins.en: Aagje Deken (1741-1804), writer. Together with Betje Wolff she wrote novels, including 'Sara Burgerhart' and 'Willem Leevend'.

origins.name: Akbarstraat
origins.en: Title of a novel by Petrus van Limburg Brouwer (1829-1873), published in 1872.

origins.name: Akerpolderstraat
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. Aker and Akerwatering are historical names that already appear on a 1687 map of Rijnland by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akersingel
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. Aker and Akerwatering are historical names that already appear on a 1687 map of Rijnland by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akersluis
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. Aker and Akerwatering are historical names that already appear on a 1687 map of Rijnland by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akerwateringstraat
origins.en: Named after the Akerpolder in the former municipality of Sloten. Aker and Akerwatering are historical names that already appear on a 1687 map of Rijnland by Jan Dou.

origins.name: Akkerdistelstraat
origins.en: An akkerdistel (creeping thistle) is a species of thistle.

origins.name: Akkerstraat
origins.en: An akker is a field of arable land, often bounded by ditches.

origins.name: Akkerwindeweg
